title: Consumer's Equilibrium
description: Class 11 Economics: utility, total and marginal utility, the law of diminishing marginal utility, consumer's equilibrium by the utility approach, and the indifference curve and budget line approach.

topics.title: Utility and the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
topics.concept:
Why does a consumer buy what he buys? Because goods give him satisfaction. In economics, the want-satisfying power of a good is called its utility. Utility is subjective — it differs from person to person and place to place (water has high utility to a thirsty traveller in a desert, low utility beside a river).

Two measures of utility are central:

  • Total Utility (TU) — the total satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a given quantity of a good.
  • Marginal Utility (MU) — the additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit of the good. MU = change in TU when one more unit is consumed.

As a person consumes more and more units of the same good, the extra satisfaction from each successive unit falls. This universal tendency is the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility (DMU): as the consumption of a good increases, its marginal utility goes on decreasing. The first slice of pizza gives great satisfaction, the second a little less, the third even less.

The table below shows this for slices of pizza:

UnitsTUMU
12020
23515
34510
4505
5500

Notice MU keeps falling (20, 15, 10, 5, 0). TU rises as long as MU is positive, is maximum when MU = 0 (the 5th unit, the point of satiety), and would fall if MU became negative.

examples.problem: Example 1: Define total utility and marginal utility.
examples.solution:
One is total, one is the extra.

  • TU = total satisfaction from a given quantity.
  • MU = the extra satisfaction from one more unit (change in TU).
examples.answer: Total utility is the total satisfaction from a quantity; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit.

examples.problem: Example 2: State the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility.
examples.solution:
Extra satisfaction falls.

  • As more units of a good are consumed, its marginal utility goes on decreasing.
examples.answer: As consumption of a good increases, the marginal utility from each additional unit goes on decreasing.

examples.problem: Example 3: In the table, why is total utility maximum at the 5th unit?
examples.solution:
Look at MU there.

  • At the 5th unit MU = 0 (the point of satiety).
  • TU is maximum when MU = 0; beyond it TU would fall.
examples.answer: Because MU = 0 at the 5th unit (point of satiety); TU is maximum when MU is zero.

recap:
• Utility = want-satisfying power of a good (subjective).
  • TU = total satisfaction; MU = extra satisfaction from one more unit (change in TU).
  • Law of DMU: as consumption rises, MU falls.
  • TU is maximum when MU = 0; TU falls if MU is negative.

quiz.q: The additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good is:
quiz.explanation: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit.

quiz.q: Total utility is maximum when marginal utility is:
quiz.explanation: TU is maximum at the point where MU = 0.

topics.title: Consumer's Equilibrium: Utility Approach
topics.concept:
A consumer is in equilibrium when he gets the maximum total satisfaction from his given income and the given prices, and has no wish to change what he buys. The utility (cardinal) approach explains this using marginal utility.

One good: if a consumer is buying a single good, he is in equilibrium where the marginal utility of the good equals its price (both measured in money):

MU = Price (P)

If MU > P, the good gives more satisfaction than it costs, so he buys more; as he buys more, MU falls (law of DMU) until MU = P. If MU < P, he buys less. Equilibrium is where they are equal.

Two or more goods: when income is spent on several goods, the consumer maximises satisfaction by the Law of Equi-Marginal Utility — he arranges his spending so that the marginal utility of the last rupee spent on each good is equal:

MUₓ ÷ Pₓ = MUₐ ÷ Pₐ = … = MU of money

In words, the satisfaction from the last rupee spent on good X should equal the satisfaction from the last rupee spent on good Y. If one good gives more utility per rupee, the consumer shifts spending toward it (its MU falls) until the ratios are equal. At that point total satisfaction is maximum and the consumer is in equilibrium. This neatly explains how a consumer with limited money divides it among many goods.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the condition for a consumer's equilibrium when buying a single good?
examples.solution:
Marginal utility equals price.

  • MU of the good = its Price (in money terms).
examples.answer: Marginal utility of the good equals its price (MU = P).

examples.problem: Example 2: If the MU of a good is greater than its price, what will the consumer do?
examples.solution:
The good is worth more than it costs.

  • He will buy more of it.
  • As he does, MU falls until MU = P.
examples.answer: He will buy more of the good (since MU > P), and his MU falls until MU = P.

examples.problem: Example 3: State the equi-marginal condition for equilibrium with two goods X and Y.
examples.solution:
Equalise utility per rupee.

  • MUₓ ÷ Pₓ = MUₐ ÷ Pₐ.
  • The last rupee on each good gives equal satisfaction.
examples.answer: MUₓ ÷ Pₓ = MUᵧ ÷ Pᵧ — the marginal utility per rupee is equal across goods.

recap:
• Consumer's equilibrium = maximum satisfaction from given income and prices.
  • One good: MU = Price (buy more if MU > P, less if MU < P).
  • Many goods (Law of Equi-Marginal Utility): MUₓ/Pₓ = MUₐ/Pₐ = … — equal MU per rupee.

quiz.q: When buying a single good, a consumer is in equilibrium where:
quiz.explanation: Single-good equilibrium is where MU equals price.

quiz.q: The Law of Equi-Marginal Utility says the consumer equalises:
options: Marginal utility per rupee across goods
quiz.explanation: Equilibrium with many goods equalises MU per rupee (MUₓ/Pₓ = MUᵧ/Pᵧ).

topics.title: Indifference Curve and Budget Line Approach
topics.concept:
A more modern approach explains the consumer without needing to measure utility in numbers — it only asks the consumer to rank combinations. It uses two tools: the indifference curve and the budget line.

An indifference curve (IC) joins all the combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same total satisfaction — so he is "indifferent" between them. Its features: it slopes downward (to keep satisfaction the same, more of one good means less of the other), it is convex to the origin, and a higher IC means more satisfaction. A set of such curves is an indifference map.

The budget line shows all the combinations of two goods a consumer can afford with his given income at the given prices. The combinations he can buy (on or below the line) form the budget set. The budget line slopes downward and its slope depends on the price ratio of the two goods.

The consumer is in equilibrium at the point where the budget line just touches (is tangent to) the highest possible indifference curve — point E below. There he buys the affordable combination that gives the maximum satisfaction.

examples.problem: Example 1: What does an indifference curve show?
examples.solution:
Same satisfaction.

  • All combinations of two goods giving the consumer the same total satisfaction.
  • He is indifferent between them.
examples.answer: An indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same total satisfaction.

examples.problem: Example 2: What does the budget line represent?
examples.solution:
What is affordable.

  • All combinations of two goods the consumer can afford with his income at the given prices.
examples.answer: The budget line shows all combinations of two goods the consumer can just afford with his given income at the given prices.

examples.problem: Example 3: Where is the consumer in equilibrium in the indifference curve approach?
examples.solution:
Highest affordable IC.

  • Where the budget line is tangent to (just touches) the highest possible indifference curve.
examples.answer: Where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve.

recap:
• Indifference curve: combinations giving the same satisfaction; downward sloping, convex to origin; higher IC = more satisfaction. Set = indifference map.
  • Budget line: combinations the consumer can afford (budget set on/below it); slope = price ratio.
  • Equilibrium: budget line tangent to the highest IC.

quiz.q: An indifference curve joins combinations of two goods giving:
quiz.explanation: An IC shows combinations of equal (same) satisfaction.

quiz.q: In the indifference curve approach, equilibrium is where the budget line is:
options: Tangent to the highest attainable IC
quiz.explanation: Equilibrium is the tangency of the budget line with the highest reachable IC.

questions.q: The want-satisfying power of a good is called its:
questions.explanation: Utility is the want-satisfying power of a good.

questions.q: Total satisfaction from a given quantity of a good is:
questions.explanation: Total utility is the total satisfaction from a quantity.

questions.q: The extra satisfaction from one more unit is:
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the satisfaction from one more unit.

questions.q: As more units of a good are consumed, its marginal utility:
questions.explanation: By the law of DMU, MU falls as consumption rises.

questions.q: Total utility is maximum when marginal utility is:
questions.explanation: TU is maximum where MU = 0 (point of satiety).

questions.q: A consumer in equilibrium gets:
options: Maximum satisfaction from given income and prices
questions.explanation: Equilibrium = maximum satisfaction from given income and prices.

questions.q: For a single good, consumer equilibrium is where:
questions.explanation: Single-good equilibrium is MU = price.

questions.q: If MU of a good exceeds its price, the consumer will:
questions.explanation: MU > P means buy more until MU = P.

questions.q: With many goods, equilibrium requires the marginal utility per rupee to be:
questions.explanation: Equi-marginal utility: MUₓ/Pₓ = MUᵧ/Pᵧ = ...

questions.q: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods giving:
questions.explanation: An IC gives the same total satisfaction.

questions.q: An indifference curve slopes:
questions.explanation: An IC slopes downward (more of one good means less of the other).

questions.q: A higher indifference curve represents:
questions.explanation: A higher IC means a higher level of satisfaction.

questions.q: The budget line shows combinations the consumer can:
questions.explanation: The budget line shows affordable combinations.

questions.q: A set of indifference curves is called an:
questions.explanation: A family of ICs is an indifference map.

questions.q: Consumer equilibrium (IC approach) is where the budget line is:
options: Tangent to the highest attainable IC
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is tangency of the budget line and the highest reachable IC.

questions.q: After eating four chocolates, the fifth gives almost no extra pleasure. This everyday experience illustrates the law of:
questions.explanation: Each additional unit yields less extra satisfaction — diminishing marginal utility.

questions.q: If TU values are 10, 18, 24, 28, 30, the marginal utility of the 4th unit is:
questions.explanation: MU of 4th unit = TU₄ − TU₃ = 28 − 24 = 4.

questions.q: A consumer finds the last rupee spent on tea gives more satisfaction than the last rupee on coffee. To maximise satisfaction he should:
options: Spend more on tea and less on coffee
questions.explanation: He shifts spending toward tea (higher MU per rupee) until MUₜ/Pₜ = MU_c/P_c.

questions.q: Water is cheap though very useful, while diamonds are dear though less useful. This paradox is explained by:
options: The low marginal utility of abundant water vs high MU of scarce diamonds
questions.explanation: Price reflects marginal, not total, utility: abundant water has low MU, scarce diamonds high MU.

questions.q: Two points on the SAME indifference curve must give the consumer:
questions.explanation: By definition, every point on one IC yields the same total satisfaction.

questions.q: If the consumer's income rises (prices unchanged), the budget line:
options: Shifts outward, parallel to the old one
questions.explanation: More income lets him afford more of both goods, shifting the budget line outward without changing its slope.

questions.q: At the 5th unit MU = 0 and TU is maximum. Consuming a 6th unit with negative MU would:
questions.explanation: Negative marginal utility means extra consumption now lowers total satisfaction.

questions.q: The downward slope of an indifference curve means that to keep satisfaction unchanged the consumer must:
options: Give up some of one good to get more of the other
questions.explanation: Gaining one good while staying equally satisfied requires sacrificing some of the other — hence the downward slope.

questions.q: The indifference curve approach is considered superior partly because it only requires the consumer to:
options: Rank combinations, not measure utility in numbers
questions.explanation: It needs only ordinal ranking of preferences, avoiding the unrealistic cardinal measurement of utility.

questions.q: A combination of goods lying ABOVE (outside) the budget line is one the consumer:
options: Cannot afford with the given income
questions.explanation: Points beyond the budget line cost more than the consumer's income allows.
